newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch flower auction devises strategy for future.
newsitem.headline: Dutch flower auction devises strategy for future.

text.p: The world's largest flower auction is engaged in a comprehensive restructuring aimed to make Dutch growers, buyers and exporters react to new international competition.

Andre Mulder, managing director, of the Dutch flower auction Bloemenveilling Aalsmeer told Reuters a new strategy devised by its management will split the auctions structure in two parts, with a range of different goals.
The first initative invites buyers from all over the world to have their flowers and plants auctioned in the Netherlands.
"International exporters and growers of flowers are now very welcome at Aalsmeer as long as they act according to the rules in respect of quality, quantity, payment and logistics," he stated.

Aalsmeers board has until recently, applied a strict criteria of rules about the boundaries across which flowers could be imported to the market and Mulder said Dutch-grown flowers have always been given priority.

New competition meant this situation could no longer prevail. "That means the members and owners of this organisation must adapt. For many, that it is a little difficult to accept as they feel that it is their market place and they have traditionally had some control over the organisation," Mulder said.
"In a second initiative, we have pledged to help all companies currently associated with Bloemenveiling Aalsmeer to market themselves more efficiently to the international marketplace."
Contact with traditional customers - such as big supermarket chains - would be enhanced and the markets doors are open to potential new customers.

"We have to convince our members that a new era has arrived and a new structure has to be created, facing bigger and bigger international production. If we really want to stay at the centre of the industry, then we have to change."

There has been little change in the market for many years since it was founded by the grandfathers of the current growers. Now it and its members must adapt and this will take roughly four years, he stated.

"We have launched our plans which are challenging and we have outlined a way ahead for the future, but to change we have to give a steady flow of concrete facts and figures about what were doing and where were all heading," he said. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
